newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia PM alleges intrigues involving Lao rebels.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia PM alleges intrigues involving Lao rebels.

text.p: Cambodian co-Premier Hun Sen on Thursday accused unnamed senior military officers of forging links with Laotian rebel exiles and warned of such an alliance ganging up against other political factions.

Vowing to destroy the Laotian rebels, Hun Sen said unidentified generals and colonels had taken the little-known Free Lao forces under their wing, put them up in luxury hotels in Phnom Penh and feted them at seaside and hill resorts.
He said the Lao rebels had turned to the unidentified officers after he refused a request one month ago to let them set up military training camps on Cambodia's border with Laos.

"This is a scandal against Lao sovereignty and independence and it has affected the friendship, trust and cooperation between Laos and Cambodia," Hun Sen said at the opening of a school in Preah Vihear province, which borders Laos.
Cambodian officials were unable to offer further information on the rebels.
Hun Sen has been close to the communist Lao government since his days as president of Cambodia's Vietnamese-backed communist regime prior to multi-party elections in 1993.

The premier said he had decided to disclose the alleged Lao activities, "because I am afraid that while Hun Sen doesn't agree (to help them) today, another day they will find another (benefactor) and he will agree."
He said he feared that whoever might serve as benefactor to the Lao rebels could use Lao fighters and Maoist Khmer Rouge defectors "as a knife" against unspecified other forces.
Right-wing rebels have operated from bases along Laos' borders with Thailand and Cambodia since the communist takeover in 1975. The origin of the Free Lao was not immediately clear.

While Hun Sen did not name potential allies of the Laotian forces, observers noted the rocky relations between Hun Sen and his co-prime minister, Prince Norodom Ranariddh, and the fact that military officers from the two leaders' rival parties have questioned each others' loyalty and honesty.

The tense relationship between the two premiers has been further strained by their competition for the allegiance of thousands of Khmer Rouge guerrillas who have defected to the coalition government in the past six months.
Hun Sen said that although he ordered the Free Lao forces destroyed in 1994 and 1995, they had approached him one month ago offering medicine worth $500,000 for health care.
He said that in exchange, "they asked me to give them some territory on the border to use for military training, including tank warfare and special forces."
He said they also offered to train Cambodian soldiers there and to supply Lao fighters to help destroy Khmer Rouge hardliners in Cambodia's north.
Hun Sen said he refused all offers.

"The Lao government has not made a fuss, but has asked us questions," said Hun Sen, who said he assured Vientiane he would take action against the Lao resistance forces just as he had done against anti-Hanoi groups in Cambodia last year.
The Cambodian government repatriated or expelled several members of two anti-Hanoi groups last year.
Laotian officials could not immediately be reached for comment.
"Please (armed forces) general staff, take care of this," the prime minister said.
